issues.subcategory: contradictory study aim
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between saying the goal is to determine whether moral incongruence generalizes to addictions broadly and saying the specific goal is to demonstrate that it is unique to sexual behavior. This creates ambiguity about whether the registered report is confirmatory, falsification-oriented, or advocacy-oriented, and may bias interpretation of equivalence/non-equivalence findings.
issues.quote: “The present work seeks to clarify if moral incongruence ... is uniquely related to sexual behavior, or if it generalizes to other addictions as well.” ... “with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.”

issues.subcategory: causal language from cross-sectional data
issues.description: The study is cross-sectional and observational, yet repeatedly uses causal language such as “contributor,” “influences,” and “affects.” Regression interactions in cross-sectional self-report data cannot establish that moral incongruence causes feelings of addiction; reverse causation and third-variable explanations remain plausible.
issues.quote: “moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction to, compulsivity in, or problems with pornography use.”

issues.subcategory: causal implications despite acknowledged limitation
issues.description: Although the limitations section acknowledges that causal inference is precluded, the hypotheses and interpretation plan still frame findings as showing that moral incongruence “predicts,” “affects,” or “influences” addiction feelings. Statistical prediction in cross-sectional data should not be interpreted as influence.
issues.quote: “despite the ability of the present study to evaluate whether or not moral incongruence affects self-reported feelings of addiction a population level”

issues.subcategory: interaction operationalization may not capture moral incongruence
issues.description: The central construct, moral incongruence, is defined solely as the product of behavior frequency and moral disapproval. This does not directly measure subjective discrepancy, conflict, distress, shame, or perceived violation of values. A person may disapprove generally but not experience personal incongruence, or may experience incongruence due to reasons not captured by a single moral-wrongness item. The construct may therefore be under-specified.
issues.quote: “moral incongruence (defined as the interaction of moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior)”

issues.subcategory: single-item moral disapproval measures
issues.description: Moral disapproval is assessed with one item per behavior. Single-item measures cannot estimate reliability, may conflate moral wrongness with legality, health concerns, stigma, religious norms, or personal preference, and may not capture the multidimensional moral evaluations relevant across pornography, gambling, alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, prescription misuse, and illicit drug use.
issues.quote: “we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions ... ‘I believe that using ________ is morally wrong’”

issues.subcategory: non-parallel moral objects across domains
issues.description: The moral-disapproval items are not conceptually parallel across domains. For alcohol, the item asks whether drinking alcohol at all is morally wrong, whereas frequency includes any alcohol use and an additional binge-drinking item; for prescription drugs, the item specifies non-medical reasons; for illegal drugs, moral disapproval may reflect legality rather than morality. Domain differences in item meaning threaten comparisons of interaction effects across behaviors.
issues.quote: “I believe that drinking alcohol is morally wrong.” ... “I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong” ... “I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.”

issues.subcategory: behavior frequency severity mismatch
issues.description: Frequency alone is treated as the behavior component of moral incongruence, but frequency has different clinical meaning across domains. Daily nicotine use, monthly gambling, and monthly illicit drug use are not comparable indicators of exposure, severity, or dysregulation. Quantity, amount wagered, intoxication level, and route of administration are omitted, weakening construct validity and cross-domain comparisons.
issues.quote: “frequency of engaging in a behavior” ... “participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day).”

issues.subcategory: modified ASSIST not validated for new scoring/use
issues.description: The authors substantially modify the ASSIST, add pornography and gambling, alter response categories, remove/alter substance categories, average standardized items rather than use validated risk scores, and apply it to behaviors for which it has not been validated. This may compromise interpretability and comparability of the dependent variables.
issues.quote: “To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST.”

issues.subcategory: ASSIST adapted to pornography/gambling without validation
issues.description: The manuscript states that pornography and gambling will be included in the NIDA-ASSIST to allow parallel analyses, while acknowledging this is not validated. Parallel formatting does not ensure construct equivalence; ASSIST items developed for substances may not function similarly for gambling or pornography.
issues.quote: “We will also include pornography and gambling as response options on the NIDA-ASSIST... Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography”

issues.subcategory: validated scales altered scoring
issues.description: The PGSI and BPS response options in the supplemental materials appear to use 0,2,4,5 for PGSI and 0,2,4 for BPS, whereas the methods describe conventional 0–3 PGSI and 0–2 BPS scoring. Changing response values affects sums/means, cutoffs, distributions, and comparability with validation studies.
issues.quote: “Problem Gambling Severity Index ... on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.” ... Supplemental table: “Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)”

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The methods report BPS responses on a 0–2 scale, but the supplemental materials list response values of 0, 2, and 4. This inconsistency would change the total score range and invalidate comparison to published BPS scoring and thresholds unless clarified.
issues.quote: “on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.” ... Supplemental table: “Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)”

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript says the PGSI uses a 0–3 response scale, while the supplemental measure lists 0,2,4,5. This is a serious internal inconsistency affecting scoring, replication, and interpretation of gambling severity.
issues.quote: “on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.” ... Supplemental table: “Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)”

issues.subcategory: wrong or ambiguous standardized effect conversion
issues.description: The manuscript equates β=.11, ΔR2=.012, f2=.016, and Cohen’s d=.25 as corresponding effect sizes, but these metrics are not generally interchangeable without specifying assumptions, model context, and conversion formula. The cited ΔR2=.012 corresponds to f2≈.012/(1-.012)=.012, not .016, if calculated directly. This affects the SESOI justification.

issues.subcategory: equivalence testing parameter mismatch
issues.description: The equivalence region is defined as δ=.11 in terms of standardized beta, but the power analyses are based on f2=.015. Equivalence testing for a regression coefficient and power to detect incremental R2/f2 are not identical. The manuscript does not justify that the f2-based power analysis adequately supports the coefficient-based Anderson-Hauck equivalence tests.
issues.quote: “We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression ... with an equivalence region ... δ= .11.” ... “power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest (f2 = .015)”

issues.subcategory: incorrect confidence interval logic for equivalence
issues.description: The manuscript says that if the confidence interval for the standardized effect falls within the equivalence region, the effect is practically null. However, equivalence testing conventionally requires an appropriate 90% CI for two one-sided tests, not necessarily a 95% CI, and Anderson-Hauck has its own test formulation. The planned CI criterion is underspecified and may not match the selected method.
issues.quote: “Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect ... fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null”

issues.subcategory: post hoc equivalence region changes
issues.description: The plan allows changing the equivalence region after observing whether effects exceed the primary SESOI and using the observed pornography effect’s confidence interval as a new benchmark. This introduces outcome-dependent analytic flexibility and undermines the confirmatory interpretation of equivalence claims across domains.
issues.quote: “In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.”

issues.subcategory: adaptive power/equivalence strategy for underpowered domains
issues.description: For low-prevalence behaviors, the authors propose switching from testing equivalence to a near-null SESOI to testing whether effects are smaller than a previously observed pornography effect. This changes the inferential question after sample-size limitations are known and could allow weak evidence to be framed as supporting uniqueness.
issues.quote: “Should we lack power to sufficient test equivalence with null effects for the above behaviors, we will adjust analyses accordingly... we would therefore not be able to evaluate equivalence with a null effect. However... we would be able to infer whether the effect of moral incongruence was less than the effect observed in previous analyses focused on pornography use.”

issues.subcategory: multiple testing not addressed for primary models
issues.description: The plan includes 10 moderation analyses plus direct effects and equivalence tests, but no multiplicity control is specified for primary hypothesis tests. This inflates the chance of false positives, especially given the central claim depends on patterns of significant versus null interactions across domains.
issues.quote: “In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest...”

issues.subcategory: Holm-adjusted test statistics wording error
issues.description: Holm adjustment applies to p-values, not test statistics. This wording suggests a misunderstanding or imprecise reporting of correlation analyses.
issues.quote: “Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics”

issues.subcategory: representativeness compromised by oversample
issues.description: The total N=4,000 combines a nationally matched sample with a sports-wagering oversample. Analyses appear to use the combined sample without specifying weighting, stratification, or sample-source adjustment. This combined sample is not representative of the U.S. population and will overrepresent gamblers/sports bettors, affecting prevalence, associations, and generalizability.
issues.quote: “the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms... we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports”

issues.subcategory: no weighting plan
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify whether YouGov survey weights will be provided or used, whether matching variables will be incorporated, or how the sports-wagering oversample will be weighted. Without this information, claims of representativeness and population-level inference cannot be evaluated.
issues.quote: “Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.”

issues.subcategory: overclaim from mixed/oversampled sample
issues.description: Despite using a sports-wagering oversample and behavior-specific subsets, the manuscript repeatedly refers to population-level inference. The analytic sample for gambling will be heavily enriched for sports bettors and may not generalize to the broader U.S. population or even to all gamblers.
issues.quote: “upcoming, nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population”

issues.subcategory: panel data quality control not transparent
issues.description: The authors rely on YouGov proprietary quality controls and state they do not anticipate removing invalid responses. However, no attention checks, speed checks, duplicate checks, straight-lining rules, exclusion criteria, or audit information are described. This limits reproducibility and quality evaluation.
issues.quote: “certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses”

issues.subcategory: unjustified assumption of no missingness
issues.description: The authors state they anticipate no unplanned missing data, but do not provide a missing-data handling plan. Online panel data can contain skipped items, breakoffs, panel-data missingness, or “prefer not to answer” responses. Lack of a prespecified strategy threatens replicability.
issues.quote: “Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.”

issues.subcategory: behavior-contingent missingness by design
issues.description: Problem-use and moral-disapproval measures are administered only to past-year users. This prevents analysis of disapproval among abstainers and conditions on behavior, potentially inducing selection/collider bias and limiting conclusions about moral disapproval in the full population.
issues.quote: “we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.”

issues.subcategory: excluding abstainers changes moral-incongruence construct
issues.description: Moral incongruence as discrepancy between values and behavior could arguably include abstainers with high disapproval as congruent cases and users with disapproval as incongruent. By excluding non-users, the design narrows the range of frequency and removes morally congruent abstainers, affecting interaction estimation and construct interpretation.
issues.quote: “key measures will be restricted to those who have engaged in the behavior within the past year.”

issues.subcategory: restricted range and zero-truncation of frequency
issues.description: Because only past-year users complete key measures, frequency predictors exclude the zero category for most primary models. Interactions between frequency and moral disapproval are estimated only among users, which can attenuate or alter interaction effects and makes conclusions about moral incongruence in the population dependent on a restricted range.
issues.quote: “only participants who report viewing pornography at least once in the past 12 months ... will complete the remaining items”

issues.subcategory: frequency scale coding inconsistency
issues.description: The methods describe frequency scales as 0–5 in some places and 1–6 in others. The supplemental materials use 0–5. This inconsistency matters for centering, interactions, interpretation, and replication.
issues.quote: “on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day)” ... “on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)”

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency measure contradiction
issues.description: The methods say gambling frequency is assessed using a single item, then says an average across gambling behaviors will be taken. The supplemental material shows only one item (“Gambled or placed bets at all”). It is unclear whether gambling frequency is a single global item or an average across multiple gambling types.
issues.quote: “We will assess gambling frequency using a single item.” ... “To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.”

issues.subcategory: number of outcomes inconsistent
issues.description: The analytic plan refers to eight proposed outcomes, but the study includes alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription misuse, illicit drugs, pornography with two outcomes, and gambling with two outcomes—nine dependent variables if pornography and gambling validated and ASSIST outcomes are separate. Later it states 10 moderation analyses for 8 target behaviors/variables, which is also inconsistent.
issues.quote: “assumptions of regression ... will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes.” ... “In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses ... corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest”

issues.subcategory: 10 moderation analyses count appears wrong
issues.description: Based on Table 1, there are five substance outcomes plus two pornography outcomes plus two gambling outcomes, totaling nine moderation analyses, unless tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine are separated or alcohol binge frequency is included separately. The stated count of 10 is not reconciled.
issues.quote: “In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest”

issues.subcategory: tobacco/non-tobacco nicotine inconsistency
issues.description: The methods say outcomes include alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, and cannabis, but the survey and Table 1 combine tobacco/nicotine products into one category. This creates ambiguity in the number and definition of substance outcomes.
issues.quote: “for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).” ... Table 1: “Tobacco/Nicotine products”

issues.subcategory: gender coding excludes nonbinary categories ambiguously
issues.description: The moderation visualization plan codes gender as binary male versus not-male. This may obscure gender diversity and introduce an ill-defined heterogeneous reference group. The manuscript does not specify how nonbinary, missing, or other gender responses will be handled in regression models.
issues.quote: “gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)”

issues.subcategory: limited covariate adjustment
issues.description: The models include only age, gender, and religiousness as covariates. Many plausible confounders may influence both moral disapproval and self-perceived addiction/problem reports, including political ideology, education, region, ethnicity, mental distress, treatment history, cultural background, and behavior-specific availability/legal status. Omitting these limits interpretation of moral-disapproval effects.
issues.quote: “we intend on including religiousness, age, and gender as covariates”

issues.subcategory: unaddressed confounding by symptom severity and stigma
issues.description: People with more severe substance/gambling problems may retrospectively increase moral disapproval due to harms, stigma, or social consequences. Thus direct and interaction effects may reflect consequence-driven moralization rather than moral incongruence producing perceived addiction. The design does not address this reverse causality/confounding.
issues.quote: “we do expect moral disapproval of substances among substance users to positively predict self-reported problems”

issues.subcategory: outcome contamination with guilt/morality items
issues.description: Some outcome measures include items directly related to guilt, failed control, or concern from others, which may overlap with moral disapproval and inflate associations. The PGSI includes a guilt item, and the BPS includes continuing pornography despite guilt. This threatens discriminant validity when testing moral disapproval as predictor of problem severity.
issues.quote: “Have you felt guilty about the way you gamble or what happens when you gamble?” ... “You continue to use pornography even though you feel guilty about it.”

issues.subcategory: self-perceived addiction versus disorder symptoms conflated
issues.description: The manuscript uses self-reported feelings of addiction, problematic use, addiction symptoms, and disorder symptoms interchangeably. Validated symptom scales and subjective perceived addiction are not identical constructs, and conclusions about diagnostic caveats require distinction between distress, perceived addiction, and clinical disorder.
issues.quote: “self-reported feelings of addiction” ... “self-reported levels of gambling disorder symptoms” ... “self-reported symptoms of substance use disorders”

issues.subcategory: substance-use disorder symptoms inadequately measured
issues.description: The modified five-item ASSIST average does not fully assess DSM/ICD substance-use disorder symptoms and is not equivalent to a diagnostic symptom count. Yet hypotheses refer to symptoms of substance use disorders. This mismatch weakens conclusions about recognized addictive disorders.
issues.quote: “We expect to find that moral incongruence, as it relates to substance use, will also not predict self-reported symptoms of substance use disorders.”

issues.subcategory: cross-domain time-frame mismatch
issues.description: Predictor frequency is measured over the past 12 months, ASSIST problem items use past 3 months plus lifetime/past-3-month items, BPS uses past 6 months, and PGSI uses past 12 months. These inconsistent time frames threaten causal ordering and comparability across outcomes.
issues.quote: “past-year frequency” ... “In the past three months...” ... “In the last 6 months...” ... “Thinking about the last 12 months…”

issues.subcategory: standardizing items before averaging mixes time frames and response scales
issues.description: The ASSIST outcome averages standardized responses across items with different response ranges and time frames, including 0–5 frequency items and 0/3/6 lifetime/past-three-month items. Standardizing item responses within sample changes item weighting and makes scores sample-dependent, reducing interpretability and comparability across substances.
issues.quote: “Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken for each substance of interest”

issues.subcategory: ordinal predictors treated as continuous without justification
issues.description: Frequency and moral disapproval are ordinal scales with few categories, but the plan treats them as continuous, centers them, and multiplies them. This may be acceptable but requires justification and sensitivity analyses because interaction terms involving ordinal variables can be scale-dependent.
issues.quote: “focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated.”

issues.subcategory: assumption testing and fallback model unclear
issues.description: The plan says that if OLS assumptions are substantially violated, they will conduct latent variable models using DWLS. However, “substantially” is undefined, not all outcomes have enough items to form latent variables, predictors remain observed ordinal variables, and latent interactions are not straightforwardly specified in lavaan with DWLS. This fallback plan is under-specified.
issues.quote: “in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses... construct latent variable models using the lavaan package... using diagonally weighted least squares estimation”

issues.subcategory: latent-variable plan impossible for single-item outcomes/predictors
issues.description: The proposed latent variable robustness approach says latent variables will be constructed for key dependent variables, but some outcomes are modified five-item composites while others are validated scales; predictors and moderators are single items. The plan does not specify indicators, identification, treatment of single-item constructs, or how the interaction will be modeled.
issues.quote: “we will construct latent variables for a key dependent variables ... and regress those latent variables on covariates, use frequency, moral disapproval, and the interaction”

issues.subcategory: insufficient sampling details
issues.description: The manuscript lacks details about recruitment invitations, response rates, eligibility criteria, quota/matching procedure, compensation, survey completion rates, and whether participants in the national and oversample groups can overlap. These are needed to assess selection bias and replicability.
issues.quote: “Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms.”

issues.subcategory: no preregistration/registered report repository details
issues.description: Although labeled a registered report and described as pre-registered, no registry, protocol link, timestamp, Stage 1 acceptance status, or deviation policy is provided in the manuscript text.
issues.quote: “Although the proposed work has many strengths (nationally representative sample, pre-registered design, rigorous statistical evaluation of hypotheses)”

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses not fully bounded
issues.description: The manuscript allows unspecified “supplemental analyses” if regression assumptions are violated and “exploratory analyses” with redefined equivalence regions. Without clear decision rules, model specifications, or reporting commitments, researcher degrees of freedom remain substantial despite the registered-report framing.
issues.quote: “we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate”

issues.subcategory: not accounting for complex sampling/weights in SEs
issues.description: If YouGov matching/weighting and an oversample are used, standard lm analyses may yield biased estimates or standard errors unless weights, strata, or sample-source variables are incorporated. The plan uses ordinary lm without specifying survey design correction.
issues.quote: “we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function in the stats package for R statistical software”

issues.subcategory: U.S. cultural context limits moral conclusions
issues.description: The study focuses on U.S. adults and a sports-wagering oversample, but conclusions are framed around diagnostic manuals and CSBD broadly. Moral norms around pornography, gambling, and substances vary substantially across countries and legal/religious contexts, limiting generalization.
issues.quote: “Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.”

issues.subcategory: ICD diagnostic caveat overinterpreted
issues.description: The manuscript treats the ICD-11 moral distress caveat as implying that moral incongruence may be unique to CSBD, but diagnostic caveats can reflect clinical controversy, historical context, or risk of overpathologizing sexuality, not empirical uniqueness versus other addictions. This weakens the theoretical premise.
issues.quote: “This distinction is only made for CSBD and not present for any other recognized diagnosis ... which suggests that moral beliefs about sexuality might play a unique role in understanding this disorder.”

issues.subcategory: uniqueness inference from null effects
issues.description: The study proposes that finding interactions only for pornography would provide strong evidence for uniqueness. However, absence of evidence in other domains may reflect measurement differences, lower reliability, restricted range, underpowered subgroups, or nonparallel outcomes rather than true theoretical uniqueness.
issues.quote: “should we find that moral incongruence ... only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model”

issues.subcategory: behavior categories too heterogeneous
issues.description: The categories “illegal/illicit drugs,” “prescription drugs for non-medical reasons,” “gambling,” and “tobacco or nicotine products” combine diverse behaviors/substances with different moral meanings, risks, use patterns, and disorder profiles. Aggregating them may obscure domain-specific effects and reduce interpretability.
issues.quote: “Illegal/Illicit Drugs” ... “Prescription Drugs for Non-Medical Reasons” ... “Tobacco or nicotine products, including cigarettes ... vape/e-cig products”

issues.subcategory: legal status confounded with moral disapproval
issues.description: For cannabis and illicit drugs, moral disapproval is likely confounded with state legal status and perceived legality. State of residence is available but not included as a covariate or moderator. This threatens interpretation of moral disapproval as personal morality rather than legal-norm endorsement.
issues.quote: “given the heterogeneity of cannabis laws in the U.S. and the now-widespread, legal use of THC”

issues.subcategory: no handling of state legality or availability
issues.description: The manuscript recognizes heterogeneity in cannabis laws but does not specify how state-level legal status, sports-betting legality, or gambling availability will be handled. These factors could affect frequency, moral disapproval, and problem reports.
issues.quote: “given the heterogeneity of cannabis laws in the U.S.”

issues.subcategory: alcohol binge item label error
issues.description: The male-specific alcohol item says “more than 5 drinks” in the prompt but the table row is labeled “More than four drinks.” This creates ambiguity in the actual survey item and sex-specific threshold.
issues.quote: “IF GENDER = MAN In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? ... More than four drinks (1)”

issues.subcategory: sex/gender threshold limitation
issues.description: The NIDA alcohol threshold is assigned by gender categories man/woman, but the manuscript does not handle nonbinary respondents or distinguish sex assigned at birth from gender identity. This may result in missing or inappropriate alcohol-risk screening for some participants.
issues.quote: “IF GENDER = WOMAN ... more than 4 drinks ... IF GENDER = MAN ... more than 5 drinks”

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency restricted to solo use
issues.description: The pornography frequency item assesses viewing pornography alone, whereas moral disapproval and BPS refer to pornography use generally. Partnered pornography use is excluded from frequency but may contribute to moral disapproval and problems, creating a mismatch.
issues.quote: “Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)”

issues.subcategory: religiousness used as covariate may overcontrol or obscure mechanism
issues.description: Religiousness is theorized as a source of moral disapproval but is included as a covariate in all models. If religiousness causally precedes moral disapproval, controlling for it may remove meaningful variance and alter the interpretation of moral disapproval effects. The causal role of religiousness is not specified.
issues.quote: “religiousness—especially conservative religiousness—is often a marker of such values” ... “religiousness, age, and gender as covariates”

issues.subcategory: covariate measurement from panel data may be temporally inconsistent
issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are taken from existing panel data rather than the survey itself. Religiousness can change and panel variables may be outdated or measured under different conditions. The manuscript does not report when these were collected or how stale/missing panel data will be handled.
issues.quote: “Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey).”

issues.subcategory: no blinding/applicable expectancy controls
issues.description: Although blinding is less central in survey research, the survey asks moral disapproval and problem-use questions in the same session with highly similar wording. No information is given about item order randomization or separation, raising concerns about priming, consistency bias, and demand characteristics.
issues.quote: “Please rate your agreement...” followed by problem-use items in the same survey battery

issues.subcategory: survey order not specified
issues.description: The order of frequency, moral disapproval, and symptom items is not fully specified. Item order could influence responses, particularly because moral judgments and guilt/problem items are closely related. Replication requires the exact order and any randomization/blocking procedures.
issues.quote: “Key measures described below are available in supplemental materials”

issues.subcategory: linear regression for skewed bounded outcomes
issues.description: Problem-use measures such as BPS, PGSI, and ASSIST composites are bounded, often zero-inflated and skewed among community samples. OLS may produce heteroscedasticity and non-normal residuals. The fallback plan is vague, and no generalized models, ordinal/count models, robust SEs, or transformations are prespecified.
issues.quote: “As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the lm function”

issues.subcategory: no explicit model equations
issues.description: The analytic plan describes moderation models but does not provide exact equations for each outcome, coding of predictors, treatment of sample weights, standardized versus unstandardized coefficients, or whether all terms are entered simultaneously. This limits reproducibility.
issues.quote: “moral disapproval ... will be tested as a moderator in the relationship between the frequency ... and self-reported problems”

issues.subcategory: power table based on total N may ignore subset-specific missing/branching
issues.description: Power estimates assume effective N equals prevalence multiplied by 4,000, but behavior-contingent administration, panel missingness, nonresponse, and oversample composition may alter Ns. For gambling, the sports-betting oversample inflates N in a nonrepresentative way. The effective N assumptions may be optimistic.
issues.quote: “Effective N ... Gambling ... 3,325”

issues.subcategory: table 2 formatting/data duplication error
issues.description: Table 2 contains repeated footnote text across multiple columns, making the table difficult to interpret and suggesting formatting or data-entry errors. This impairs review of the power analysis values.
issues.quote: “1. All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey... | 1. All substance estimates based...”

issues.subcategory: ethics and consent not described
issues.description: The methods do not describe IRB/ethics approval, informed consent, participant protections, or handling of sensitive sexual/substance-use data. These are essential for evaluating ethical conduct and replicability.
issues.quote: “Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study...”

issues.subcategory: clinical diagnostic implications from nonclinical self-report sample
issues.description: The manuscript proposes implications for CSBD diagnosis and false-positive diagnoses, but the study uses a general population/online panel, not clinical interviews or treatment-seeking samples. This limits conclusions about diagnostic criteria and clinical false positives.
issues.quote: “there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD.”

issues.subcategory: self-report bias central and unmitigated
issues.description: All focal variables are self-reported in a single survey, including morally sensitive behaviors and symptoms. Social desirability, shame, recall bias, and common-method variance may inflate associations between moral disapproval and problem reports. No validity checks or alternative informants/clinical assessments are included.
issues.quote: “self-reported feelings of addiction” ... “Participants will respond...”

issues.subcategory: no plan for subgroup reliability/invariance
issues.description: The study compares effects across behaviors and likely across gender/religiosity subgroups, but does not test measurement invariance or differential item functioning for BPS, PGSI, or modified ASSIST across groups. Cross-domain and subgroup comparisons may be biased by measurement non-equivalence.
issues.quote: “Descriptive statistics ... as well as measures of internal consistency ... will be calculated”

issues.subcategory: internal consistency inappropriate for heterogeneous ASSIST composite
issues.description: Cronbach’s alpha and omega may not be meaningful for the modified ASSIST composite because items capture different symptom domains and time frames rather than interchangeable indicators of one latent factor. Reporting reliability alone does not validate averaging.
issues.quote: “measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach’s alpha and Omega total)”

issues.subcategory: moral distress and moral disapproval conflated
issues.description: ICD-11 refers to distress related to moral judgments, but the study measures moral disapproval and not distress caused by moral conflict. Conclusions about the diagnostic caveat for moral distress may therefore be unsupported by the measured construct.
issues.quote: “distress related to moral objections about sexual behavior should not be taken as a symptom” ... “Moral disapproval of pornography will be assessed... ‘I believe that pornography use is morally wrong’”

issues.subcategory: direct effect of moral disapproval among users not moral incongruence
issues.description: The hypotheses include direct effects of moral disapproval among users as evidence-relevant, but the introduction itself argues that direct effects may merely reflect two negative judgments about the same behavior and are not proof of moral incongruence. This inconsistency weakens interpretation of direct-effect hypotheses.
issues.quote: “Direct effects of moral disapproval of a behavior on feelings of addiction to that behavior may not be proof that moral incongruence is driving feelings of addiction.” ... “We expect to find that the simple, direct effect of moral disapproval...”

issues.subcategory: interaction effect compared across outcomes with different scaling/reliability
issues.description: The central uniqueness claim depends on comparing standardized interaction coefficients across different outcomes and measures. Standardized coefficients vary with outcome variance, predictor variance, reliability, and sample composition, so differences across domains may not reflect differences in theoretical effect size.
issues.quote: “whether moral incongruence ... only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography”

issues.subcategory: no plan for comparing interactions statistically across domains
issues.description: The manuscript plans separate moderation/equivalence tests for each domain but does not prespecify a formal test comparing interaction effects between pornography and other behaviors within the same model or via dependent-coefficient methods. Claims of uniqueness require direct comparative tests, not only one significant and others null/equivalent.
issues.quote: “Interactions between moral disapproval and behavioral frequency will be tested for a variety of behaviors ... to establish whether...”

issues.subcategory: significance-versus-equivalence asymmetry
issues.description: The hypotheses for pornography rely on significance of a positive interaction, whereas hypotheses for other domains rely on equivalence to near-zero. Because measures, reliabilities, and sample sizes differ, this asymmetric decision rule may not fairly support uniqueness unless direct comparative and measurement-equivalence evidence is provided.
issues.quote: “we expect ... interaction ... will positively predict...” ... “we anticipate that equivalence tests will reveal the effect ... to fall within the equivalence interval”

issues.subcategory: branching only users but moral disapproval may affect nonuse
issues.description: By administering moral disapproval only to people who engaged in the behavior, the study cannot evaluate whether moral disapproval suppresses behavior frequency or creates abstinence. This can distort observed interactions among users and misses a key part of value-behavior congruence.
issues.quote: “we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.”

issues.subcategory: underpowered low-prevalence substance subgroups
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges insufficient power for prescription drug misuse and possibly illicit substances. Any null/equivalence conclusions for these domains will be weak, especially given small effective Ns and likely heterogeneity of substances.
issues.quote: “it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small”

issues.subcategory: equivalence tests underpowered for small subgroups
issues.description: Equivalence testing generally requires larger samples than null-hypothesis significance testing. The manuscript’s low expected Ns for prescription misuse and illicit drug use make near-null equivalence claims especially fragile, and the proposed alternative equivalence region changes the research question rather than solving the problem.
issues.quote: “Prescription Drug Misuse ... Effective N 140 ... Estimated Achieved power for f2=.015 .301”

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency item ignores intensity/expenditure
issues.description: Gambling disorder risk depends heavily on money wagered, losses, type of gambling, and duration, not merely frequency. A person buying a weekly lottery ticket differs from a weekly high-stakes sports bettor, but both may receive the same frequency score. This weakens tests of gambling moral incongruence.
issues.quote: “Participants will be asked how often they have engaged in the behavior over the past 12 months using the same 6-point scale”

issues.subcategory: alcohol frequency ignores quantity for main analysis
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that alcohol frequency will be measured generally without quantity, even though alcohol-related problems depend strongly on quantity and binge episodes. Using any-drinking frequency may misclassify low-risk frequent drinkers and high-risk infrequent binge drinkers.
issues.quote: “we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).”

issues.subcategory: gender-specific alcohol threshold inconsistency with stated inclusion
issues.description: The manuscript says the original NIDA Quick Screen binge-drinking response options will be included, but the planned analyses use general alcohol frequency. It is unclear whether binge-drinking variables will be analyzed, used for screening, or ignored.
issues.quote: “Although we will include these response options, for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally”

issues.subcategory: dependent-variable choice ambiguity for pornography/gambling
issues.description: Pornography and gambling each have both modified ASSIST outcomes and validated outcomes, but the hypotheses do not clearly specify which outcome is primary for confirming each hypothesis. Multiple outcomes increase analytic flexibility and complicate interpretation if results diverge.
issues.quote: “Pornography Use | Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score and modified NIDA-ASSIST items” ... “Gambling Behavior | Problem Gambling Severity Index and modified NIDA-ASSIST items”

issues.subcategory: primary outcome not clearly designated
issues.description: For pornography and gambling, there are two outcomes each, but no hierarchy or rule for resolving conflicting results. Claims about whether moral incongruence is unique could depend on selecting the outcome that supports the hypothesis.
issues.quote: “pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use”

issues.subcategory: validated typo and measure status
issues.description: The phrase “validate measures” appears to mean “validated measures.” More importantly, it contrasts validated measures with modified ASSIST measures but does not specify how conflicting results will be prioritized.
issues.quote: “the validate measures of problematic use”

issues.subcategory: no data/code availability plan
issues.description: The manuscript does not state whether deidentified data, analysis scripts, survey instruments, and codebooks will be shared. This is especially important for a registered report with complex recoding and modified measures.
issues.quote: “Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format.”

issues.subcategory: funding context may affect design but no COI statement
issues.description: The study is funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming and embedded in a larger sports-wagering project. The manuscript does not provide a conflict-of-interest or funder-role statement, relevant given gambling outcomes and oversampling.
issues.quote: “funded by the International Center for Responsible Gaming”

issues.subcategory: pornography as addiction compared with recognized disorders
issues.description: The manuscript compares self-reported pornography addiction/problematic use with recognized addictive disorders, but pornography addiction is not a recognized disorder and CSBD is not synonymous with pornography addiction. The conceptual bridge from pornography measures to CSBD is therefore limited.
issues.quote: “recognized addictive disorders such as gambling and substance use disorders ... with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.”

issues.subcategory: CSBD conflated with pornography use
issues.description: The study’s sexual behavior domain is pornography use only, yet the discussion frames implications for CSBD and sexual behaviors broadly. CSBD can involve diverse sexual behaviors, and pornography-specific moral incongruence may not generalize to CSBD.
issues.quote: “unique to sexual behaviors, particularly pornography use” ... “Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant ... for sexual behaviors”

issues.subcategory: no clinical diagnosis validation
issues.description: The study relies on screening scales and self-reports without clinical interviews or diagnostic assessment. Therefore, it cannot directly assess whether moral distress would produce false-positive diagnoses of CSBD, gambling disorder, or substance use disorder.
issues.quote: “self-reported problems with or addiction to that behavior”

issues.subcategory: no exclusion/inclusion criteria beyond age and behavior
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify eligibility criteria such as age verification, U.S. residence, language proficiency, duplicate participation, or whether participants in the sports-wagering oversample are excluded from the representative sample. This limits replicability.
issues.quote: “Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling”

issues.subcategory: independence assumption may be violated by repeated outcomes within participants
issues.description: The plan runs separate regressions for each behavior, but responses for multiple behaviors are nested within participants and likely correlated. Separate models do not account for within-person dependence when making cross-domain comparisons. A multilevel or multivariate framework may be more appropriate for testing generalization.
issues.quote: “for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample”

issues.subcategory: no plan for overlap among substance users
issues.description: Many participants will use multiple substances/behaviors. The models do not control for comorbid behaviors or specify whether frequency/problem reports in other domains will be included, despite comorbidity potentially confounding associations between moral disapproval and perceived addiction.
issues.quote: “a variety of other behavioral addiction symptoms, substance use behaviors, and general mental well-being”

issues.subcategory: comorbidity confounding not addressed
issues.description: General distress, impulsivity, or addiction liability could cause both higher problem scores across domains and moral self-condemnation. Without controlling for comorbidity or mental health, domain-specific moral effects may be confounded.
issues.quote: “how those behaviors relate to a wide variety of other behavioral addiction symptoms, substance use behaviors, and general mental well-being”

issues.subcategory: centered interaction but equivalence on standardized effect unclear
issues.description: The plan centers predictors but does not state whether variables will be standardized before interaction, whether coefficients tested for equivalence are standardized post hoc, and how standardized interaction coefficients will be computed. Standardized interaction coefficients are sensitive to scaling and centering choices.
issues.quote: “key variables will be centered ... and their product will be computed.” ... “observed standardized effect of the interaction”

issues.subcategory: decision rules for assumption violations missing
issues.description: The authors list regression assumptions but do not specify diagnostic tests, thresholds, or what constitutes substantial violation. This leaves flexibility in whether to report OLS or alternative models.
issues.quote: “should basic assumptions of regression be violated substantially”

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval of use versus misuse
issues.description: For some domains, moral disapproval of any use may differ from moral disapproval of problematic/excessive use. The study asks whether using alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, gambling, or pornography is morally wrong, not whether excessive or harmful use is wrong. This may produce floor/ceiling effects and poor alignment with problem outcomes.
issues.quote: “I believe that gambling is morally wrong.” ... “I believe that drinking alcohol is morally wrong.”

issues.subcategory: potential ceiling effects for illicit/prescription misuse disapproval
issues.description: Moral disapproval of illegal/illicit drugs and prescription drug misuse may be near ceiling among users, reducing variance and interaction power. The analytic plan does not address range restriction or ceiling effects, which could falsely support null/equivalence conclusions.
issues.quote: “I believe that using prescription drugs for non-medical reasons is morally wrong” ... “I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.”

issues.subcategory: outcome includes external concern item that may reflect others' morality
issues.description: The ASSIST-derived outcome includes whether others expressed concern. This may reflect family/community moral norms rather than the participant’s addictive symptoms, especially for pornography, gambling, or substances in moralized environments, inflating associations with moral disapproval.
issues.quote: “Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?”

issues.subcategory: survey context priming sports wagering
issues.description: Because the larger study focuses on sports wagering, participants—especially the oversample—may be primed to think about gambling harms or morality, potentially affecting gambling responses. No information is provided on survey order or mitigation.
issues.quote: “The primary focus of this project is to assess the prevalence of sports-wagering behaviors...”

issues.subcategory: sample size described as over 4,000 but exactly targeted 4,000
issues.description: The manuscript says the design will provide a total sample of over 4,000, but the stated target samples are 2,500 and 1,500, totaling exactly 4,000. This is a minor numerical inconsistency.
issues.quote: “This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.”

issues.subcategory: no handling of participants with no past-three-month use
issues.description: Past-year users complete problem items referring to past three months. Participants who used in the past year but not past three months may answer problem items as zero, while lifetime/ever control items may be positive. The scoring plan does not address interpretation of mixed time-frame responses.
issues.quote: “Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.” ... “In the past three months...”

issues.subcategory: OLS with small low-prevalence samples and many predictors
issues.description: For prescription misuse, projected n=140 with six predictors and potentially skewed outcomes may produce unstable interaction estimates and wide confidence intervals. Equivalence or non-equivalence conclusions in this subgroup will be unreliable.
issues.quote: “Prescription Drug Misuse ... Effective N 140”

issues.subcategory: religiousness as unique source of pornography moral incongruence overclaimed
issues.description: The manuscript states evidence supports moral incongruence in pornography as uniquely related to religious values, but the study measures moral disapproval directly and does not test other moral foundations, feminist/ethical objections, exploitation concerns, or relationship norms. This overstates the theoretical specificity of religion.
issues.quote: “Taken together, these findings provide strong evidence for the argument that moral incongruence in the context of pornography use is likely uniquely related to religious values.”

issues.subcategory: lack of item-level supplemental for all modified ASSIST scoring details
issues.description: Although items are shown, the manuscript does not specify whether item standardization is within the whole sample, within users, by substance, or across all substances, nor how missing/branching values are handled. This is necessary to reproduce ASSIST composites.
issues.quote: “Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken for each substance”

issues.subcategory: using average PGSI instead of validated sum/cutoffs
issues.description: The PGSI is typically summed and interpreted using established categories. Averaging may be linearly equivalent if conventional scoring is used, but with altered 0/2/4/5 scoring and no cutoff use, comparability with validation studies and severity categories is reduced.
issues.quote: “Responses will be averaged.”

issues.subcategory: BPS sum score with altered response values affects validation
issues.description: The BPS validation uses specific scoring. If the supplemental 0/2/4 response values are used, the sum score range doubles, and validated cutoffs/sensitivity/specificity no longer apply unless rescaled.
issues.quote: “Brief Pornography Screen Sum Score” ... “Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)”

issues.subcategory: no manipulation or temporal ordering for moderation interpretation
issues.description: The interaction between frequency and moral disapproval is interpreted as moral disapproval amplifying the frequency-problem relationship, but both variables and outcomes are measured contemporaneously. Moderation direction is theoretical rather than established; problem severity could moderate reported disapproval or frequency reporting.
issues.quote: “moral disapproval of pornography likely amplifies the links between pornography use and self-reported feelings of compulsivity or addiction.”

issues.subcategory: sports bettors overrepresented in substance estimates
issues.description: Sports bettors may differ from the general population in substance use, risk-taking, demographics, and moral views. Combining them with the representative sample may distort substance-use analyses as well, not only gambling analyses.
issues.quote: “an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports”

issues.subcategory: no plan to include sample source as covariate/moderator
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify whether national sample versus sports-wagering oversample membership will be included in analyses. Sample source could confound gambling frequency, moral disapproval, and problem gambling symptoms.
issues.quote: “we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent ... history of wagering on sports”

issues.subcategory: dependent-variable non-independence due to duplicated pornography/gambling measures
issues.description: Pornography and gambling are each assessed with two outcomes. If both are analyzed without accounting for their correlation, conclusions may double-count evidence for those domains relative to substance domains.
issues.quote: “pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures”

issues.subcategory: recognized disorder comparison excludes gaming despite critique focus
issues.description: The critique motivating the study includes gaming and internet/social media moral disapproval, but the proposed study omits gaming disorder while including substances and gambling. This is defensible but limits the ability to address the full critique about behavioral addictions.
issues.quote: “other so-called addictive behaviors (e.g., gaming and internet use)” ... “gambling and substance use disorders”

issues.subcategory: substance prevalence estimates may not match analytic definitions
issues.description: Power estimates use NSDUH prevalence for substance categories, but analytic definitions include modified broad categories such as any alcohol frequency, tobacco/nicotine products, cannabis/THC, and nonmedical prescription drug use. If definitions differ from NSDUH estimates, projected Ns and power may be inaccurate.
issues.quote: “All substance estimates based on the 2019-2020 National Survey on Drug Use and Health”

issues.subcategory: prescription drug misuse frequency item excludes prescribed problematic use
issues.description: The study assesses prescription drugs only for non-medical reasons, which omits problematic use of prescribed medications taken medically but compulsively or at higher doses. This narrows the construct of prescription drug problems.
issues.quote: “Prescription Drugs for Non-Medical Reasons”

issues.subcategory: no specification of illicit drug examples
issues.description: The “illegal/illicit drugs” category is not defined with examples. Participants may interpret cannabis differently depending on state legality, may include or exclude psychedelics, cocaine, methamphetamine, opioids, or nonmedical prescriptions, reducing reliability.
issues.quote: “Illegal/Illicit Drugs”

issues.subcategory: equivalence region based on pornography prior may bias uniqueness test
issues.description: The SESOI is derived from prior pornography-use interactions. Using pornography-specific literature to define the threshold for non-pornography domains may prejudge what counts as meaningful for substances or gambling, where clinically meaningful interaction sizes may differ.
issues.quote: “we elected to set our SESOI ... equal to the observed standardized estimate ... [from] an interaction between religiousness ... and pornography viewing frequency”

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval not necessarily moral incongruence for illegal behaviors
issues.description: For illegal drugs or prescription misuse, disapproval may be normative/legal rather than personally value-incongruent. Users may disapprove of “illegal drugs” generally but not of their own specific use. This undermines the cross-domain comparison with pornography moral incongruence.
issues.quote: “I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong.”

issues.subcategory: no attention to legal sports betting state differences
issues.description: Sports wagering legality and accessibility vary by state, influencing frequency and moral/legal attitudes. State is available in panel data but no adjustment is planned.
issues.quote: “State of Residence”

issues.subcategory: survey timing outdated/unclear relative to registered report
issues.description: The methods state participants will be recruited in late March 2022, but the manuscript is presented as an upcoming registered report. If data have already been collected, Stage 1 registration status and data access/blinding must be clarified.
issues.quote: “Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022”

issues.subcategory: possible data already collected in registered report
issues.description: Because recruitment is specified for March 2022, it is unclear whether the data existed or were accessible at the time of registration/review. Registered reports require that hypotheses and analyses be specified before outcome data are known; this needs explicit assurance.
issues.quote: “The present work seeks to ... make use of an upcoming study” ... “Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022”
